query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermal processing route that inverts the brittle, continuous phase of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 into a microstructure with a continuous ductile matrix and finely dispersed caloric-phase precipitates will enhance mechanical integrity (reducing cracking) while retaining the high field‐induced caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 in its as-synthesized state shows excellent caloric response under applied field and pressure but suffers from poor integrity with brittle cracking due to a continuous, inherently brittle intermetallic phase.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid solution treatment immediately after synthesis followed by a controlled, moderate-temperature annealing sequence aimed at inducing phase inversion. This heat-treatment is designed to decompose the continuous brittle phase into fine, discrete precipitates embedded in a ductile matrix.
generation.conditions: Processing in an inert atmosphere at temperatures below the onset of caloric-phase transformation, with a rapid quench after solution treatment to freeze high-temperature states, then annealing at moderate temperatures for controlled time durations. Operational use remains under applied field or pressure at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: An inverted microstructure wherein a continuous ductile phase (likely a disordered BCC or FCC structure) serves as the load-bearing matrix while the original caloric-phase forms as fine, uniformly distributed precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The heat treatment promotes phase separation: the originally continuous brittle phase segregates into fine precipitates, disrupting crack propagation and enhancing toughness. Meanwhile, the ductile matrix retains the field-induced phase change capability necessary for caloric effects. This rearrangement improves load transfer and integrity without disturbing the caloric mechanism active in the precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to raise compressive (and tensile) strength above the levels achieved with epoxy or low-melting agent composites (targeting >220 MPa), reduce cracking, and maintain a caloric response within 10% of the original performance under applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
generation.baseline: Prior routes using epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe achieved compressive strengths of 152–218 MPa and In composites reached only 48 MPa with improved heat transport, but neither strategy provided robust mechanical integrity alongside high caloric performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only when the annealing temperature and duration are carefully controlled to avoid excessive phase coarsening or alteration of the transformation temperatures; it is applicable for operations under ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and under the same applied-field/pressure conditions as the untreated alloy.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how sensitive the caloric transformation is to the modified microstructure and whether the new phase distribution might slightly shift the transformation temperatures. Quantitative effects on the caloric entropy change need to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize multiple batches of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 and subject them to a rapid solution treatment followed by a series of controlled annealing treatments (varying temperature and time). Characterize the resulting microstructure (SEM/TEM and XRD) and measure mechanical properties via compressive and tensile tests. Evaluate the caloric performance using field‐induced (or pressure‐induced) caloric effect measurements.
measurements: Phase composition and grain/precipitate size distribution (via SEM/TEM, XRD)
Mechanical integrity: compressive and tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness
Caloric effect: temperature change or entropy change under a defined applied field/pressure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical strength (e.g., compressive strength increase of at least 10% compared to epoxy composite specimens) while maintaining a caloric response within 10% of that of the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (Al 14.8 Co 21.3 Cr 21.3 Fe 21.3 Ni 21.3 at. %). Test conditions: Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.
